terms.definition: A planet made mostly of rock and metal with a solid surface — Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.
terms.function: Defines the inner-planet family: small, dense, and close to the Sun.
terms.whereItIs: Tagged over the inner four cards of the deck.
terms.whyItMatters: All four rocky worlds are small compared with the giant planets, which is why the family tag exists.

terms.definition: A huge planet made mostly of hydrogen and helium with no solid surface near its clouds — Jupiter and Saturn.
terms.function: Marks the two largest planets as a distinct family from the rocky worlds.
terms.whereItIs: Tagged over the Jupiter and Saturn cards; Jupiter's card is the largest in the deck.
terms.whyItMatters: Gas giants hold most of the mass in the solar system outside the Sun, yet have nothing to stand on.

terms.definition: A planet made mostly of icy materials — water, ammonia, and methane — over a rocky core: Uranus and Neptune.
terms.function: Separates Uranus and Neptune from the gas giants in the deck's family tags.
terms.whereItIs: Tagged over the Uranus and Neptune cards at the right end of the fan.
terms.whyItMatters: Ice giants look similar to gas giants but have a genuinely different composition, so they get their own family.

terms.definition: The time a planet takes to spin once around its own axis — the length of one day on that world.
terms.function: Explains why day length appears as a row on every card: each planet spins at its own speed.
terms.whereItIs: A row on every card; Jupiter's 9.9-hour day is the shortest in the deck.
terms.whyItMatters: Day length is decided by spin, not by size or distance — the biggest planet has the shortest day.

terms.definition: The time a planet takes to complete one full orbit of the Sun.
terms.function: Explains why the year row grows steadily as the deck moves outward from the Sun.
terms.whereItIs: A row on every card, growing from Mercury's 88 days to Neptune's ~165 Earth years.
terms.whyItMatters: Year length is decided by distance from the Sun — the farther a planet orbits, the longer its year.
